stops.name: La Paz, the revolution observed
stops.campa: The train climbs into the Bolivian altiplano and drops the travelers into a city boiling with the aftermath of the 1952 revolution: miners with slung rifles in the streets, the MNR handing out land and votes, Indian peasants entering ministries that had never let them past the door. Ernesto watches with the skeptic's eye. He sees the DDT sprayed on peasants in the ministry waiting room and pronounces the revolution incomplete. In the diary of this second journey La Paz appears as a splendid, turbulent lesson in what half-revolutions look like.
stops.quote: La Paz is the Shanghai of the Americas.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Guevara, diary of the second journey (Otra vez / Back on the Road), July 1953

stops.name: Bolsa Negra, the wolfram mine
stops.campa: With Calica he rides out to the state wolfram mine at Bolsa Negra, high under the glaciers of Mururata, to see the revolution where it works. The miners, the same class that stormed La Paz with dynamite, show the visitors the tunnels, the thin air, the short lives. Ernesto descends into the mountain and comes up with the conviction that here, not in the ministries, lives the real force of Bolivia. Thirteen years later he will come back to this country to bet his life on that conviction, and lose it.

stops.name: Guayaquil, the swerve toward Guatemala
stops.campa: In the humid river port of Guayaquil, camped in a boarding house with a floating population of Argentine wanderers, the plan dissolves and re-forms. Ricardo Rojo and the others are heading for Guatemala, where Colonel Árbenz is expropriating the United Fruit Company and building something unheard of. Venezuela and the waiting Granado lose the coin toss of history: Ernesto scrapes a free passage and swings north. The canon marks Guayaquil as the hinge: the place where the itinerary of a curious doctor became the trajectory of a revolutionary.

stops.name: San José de Costa Rica, the Moncada veterans and the oath before Stalin
stops.campa: Crossing Central America on foot, by boat and banana truck, through Panama and the United Fruit dominions that he studies like enemy terrain, Ernesto reaches San José. In the exile cafés he meets survivors of the assault on the Moncada barracks in Cuba, who tell him of a jailed young lawyer named Fidel Castro; he argues with Rómulo Betancourt and takes the measure of the reformists. From here he writes his aunt Beatriz the letter with the oath: he has seen the octopus, and he has sworn before the image of Stalin not to rest until it is destroyed.
stops.quote: Along the way, I had the opportunity to pass through the dominions of the United Fruit, convincing me once again of just how terrible these capitalist octopuses are. I have sworn before a picture of the old and mourned comrade Stalin that I won't rest until I see these capitalist octopuses annihilated.
stops.quote_source: Letter from Ernesto Guevara to his aunt Beatriz, San José, 10 December 1953

stops.name: Guatemala City: Hilda, and the school of revolution
stops.campa: He arrives on Christmas Eve into the one country in America where the reform is real: Árbenz's Guatemala, land deeds moving to peasants, United Fruit howling to Washington. Penniless, selling encyclopedias and images of the Lord of Esquipulas, he meets Hilda Gadea, Peruvian APRA exile, economist, reader of Mao, who feeds him, lends him books and debates him into sharper politics. Here, among exiles of every defeated Latin American cause, someone first calls the mate-drinking Argentine 'Che'. The name enters the world in Guatemala, waiting for its bearer to grow into it.

stops.name: Guatemala City, the fall of Árbenz
stops.campa: The CIA's planes come over the city dropping bombs and leaflets, and Castillo Armas's mercenary column walks in from Honduras. Ernesto runs through the blacked-out streets hauling weapons, urging the government to arm the people and fight; he signs up for the militias that are never mustered. On the twenty-seventh of June Árbenz resigns without a battle, and the young doctor watches a democracy die of moderation. The lesson burns into him permanently: a revolution that will not defend itself with arms is a revolution already lost. Hunted, he takes asylum in the Argentine embassy.
stops.quote: It was all a lot of fun, what with the bombs, speeches and other distractions to break the monotony I was living in.
stops.quote_source: Letter from Ernesto Guevara to his mother, Guatemala, June-July 1954

stops.name: Mexico City, the photographer of the plazas
stops.campa: The defeated of Guatemala wash up in Mexico City, and Ernesto among them, on the twenty-first of September. He survives as a street photographer in the plazas and an allergy researcher at the General Hospital, climbing volcanoes on weekends: again and again he assaults Popocatépetl, asthma against altitude, and calls it training. Hilda arrives; they marry and a daughter, Hildita, is born. Mexico is the antechamber: the city of Trotsky's tomb now hosts, in its cheap apartments, the future general staff of the Cuban Revolution, not yet assembled.

stops.name: Mexico City, Calle Emparan 49, the night with Fidel
stops.campa: In July 1955 Raúl Castro brings his newly amnestied brother to the apartment of María Antonia González at Emparan 49, and Ernesto Guevara meets Fidel Castro. They talk from evening until dawn of Cuba, America, the coming expedition against Batista, and by sunrise the Argentine doctor is enrolled as the invasion's physician, the third confirmed member after the brothers themselves. The diary records the encounter with cool astonishment. The canon records it as the conjunction: the strategist and the prophet of the deed have found each other, ten hours of talk sealing twelve years of war.
stops.quote: A political event is having met Fidel Castro, the Cuban revolutionary, a young, intelligent guy, very sure of himself and extraordinarily audacious; I think we hit it off well.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Guevara, Mexico diary entry, July 1955

stops.name: Rancho San Miguel, Chalco, the guerrilla academy
stops.campa: On a dusty ranch outside Chalco, the Spanish Civil War veteran Colonel Alberto Bayo drills Fidel's eighty-odd recruits in marksmanship, night marches and the theory of the guerrilla. The asthmatic Argentine outmarches, outshoots and outstudies the Cubans; Bayo names him the best student of the class, and Fidel promotes him from doctor to soldier. On the crags of Iztaccíhuatl and in the ranch's dry hills, the man now called Che completes the transformation begun at Valparaíso and Baquedano: the stethoscope will board the boat, but next to a rifle.

stops.name: Mexico City, Miguel Schultz immigration prison
stops.campa: Mexican police sweep up the conspirators in June; Che, taken with cannon evidence of the plot and an unashamed Marxist tongue, is held in the Miguel Schultz street prison longer than nearly all the others. Fidel, released first, refuses to sail without him, 'I will not abandon you,' and the canon counts the vow among Fidel's debts of honor. From his cell the prisoner writes to his parents the letter of farewell to ordinary life, embracing struggle with the fatalism of a man who has already seen his road to the end.
stops.quote: I am not Christ or a philanthropist... I fight for the things I believe in, with all the weapons at my disposal, and try to leave the other man dead so that I don't get nailed to a cross or any other place.
stops.quote_source: Letter from Ernesto Guevara to his parents, Mexico, July 1956

stops.name: Tuxpan, the embarkation of the eighty-two
stops.campa: At half past one in the morning of the twenty-fifth of November, in rain and a norther that has closed the port, eighty-two men file aboard a white pleasure yacht built for twelve, its name a grandmother's endearment: Granma. Lights out, engines low, she slips down the Tuxpan river past the sleeping harbor watch and out into the heaving Gulf. Che is aboard as troop doctor with his asthma inhalers and a rifle. Fidel has promised Cuba a rising for the last days of November; the sea will decide the punctuality.

stops.name: The Gulf and the Caribbean, seven days of the Granma
stops.campa: For seven days the little yacht wallows through heavy seas, bilge pumps failing, eighty-two revolutionaries packed among fuel drums, nearly all of them helplessly seasick. They sing the national anthem as they clear Mexican waters, then fall silent for a week of vomit, thirst and cold spray. Che, doctor of the expedition, can offer almost nothing; he records the crossing with clinical mercy. The landing date passes with the boat still at sea. In Santiago, Frank País's rising flares and dies alone. The Granma arrives late to its own legend, which only deepens it.
stops.quote: The entire boat took on an aspect both ridiculous and tragic: men clutching their stomachs, anguish written on their faces, some with their heads in buckets, others lying immobile in the strangest positions.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War, on the Granma crossing
